subject: sociology
title: Crime & Deviance: Marxism & Interactionism
welcome_lead: Capitalism criminogenic — and the powerful write the rules.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology crime: Marxism Chambliss, interactionism Becker labelling.
final_note: Crime is constructed by both economy and labels.

walkthroughs.body_html: Marxists like Chambliss (1976) see capitalism as criminogenic — its competition, inequality and frustration drive crime at all levels. The law protects property and ruling-class interests. Snider (1993): corporate crime costs far more than street crime but is rarely prosecuted.

Becker (1963): 'Deviance is not a quality of the act but of the label.' Once labelled, individuals undergo secondary deviance (Lemert) — the label becomes a master status shaping a deviant career. Cicourel (1968): police use 'typifications' that disproportionately label working-class youth.

Cohen (1972) analysed media coverage of mods and rockers in 1964. Press exaggerated, sensitised public, amplified police response — creating a deviancy amplification spiral. Cohen identified four folk devils: stages of media construction of villains.

It is treated more harshly than street crime.

mcqs.q: According to Becker, what makes an act deviant?
options: Being labelled as deviant by others - deviance is in the reaction, not the act.
Breaking a law makes any act deviant.
Acts are objectively deviant regardless of context.
It is treated more harshly than street crime.

mcqs.q: What is Merton's strain theory of crime?
options: Strain theory says people commit crime because they are stressed.

Crime results from a mismatch between cultural goals (success, wealth) and legitimate means of achieving them — those who can't access legitimate means may innovate (crime), ritualise, retreat or rebel.
Strain theory says criminals have psychological strain disorders.
It is treated more harshly than street crime.
